newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds ease back over worries in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds ease back over worries in Europe.

text.p: Irish bonds eased back on Thursday in line with other European markets as worries over the German government's plans to revalue gold reserves and continuing fears about France's looming general election took their toll on sentiment, dealers said.

"The unease in Europe is pushing bond prices back again today," a dealer said. "The market reaction to the German situation is that the German government will win the battle and push ahead with revaluation -- and that means a fudged euro."
The German government intends to use the funds raised from the revaluation to reduce its debts so that it can qualify for EMU.
However, a fudged euro would be favourable to peripheral markets, dealers said, as the base for entry would be broadened. The main consideration however, was that EMU started according to schedule.
"Irish bonds have narrowed their spreads today and, along with other peripheral markets, are outperforming Germany," a dealer said."
By 1510 GMT the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 22 pence at 101.85 to yield 5.99 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was down 20 pence at 108.50 to yield 6.72 percent.

Dealers said that Irish bond yields against German bunds had narrowed from the previous close, with the yield against Germany at 136 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 82 over in the 10-year -- a tightening of four basis points.

Rumours on Wednesday that private opinion polls were showing the French socialists in line for a win spooked the markets because of fears the left will be less willing to make sacrifices to achieve European monetary union.
The long end of the curve was hit as expectations were raised of a softer euro, an effect compounded by worries over the German government's intention to revalue.
Dealers said trade activity had been dampened on Thursday by the market holiday in Germany.
